Summary:

This is a nice study that tackles an interesting question: namely, does the quaternary structure of an ancestral protein constrain the evolution of subsequent paralogs? The central hypothesis of the paper is that, in cases where the ancestral protein is homomeric, selection to maintain binding interfaces between newly duplicated paralogs will lead to a decrease in the rate of functional divergence of those genes.

In testing this hypothesis, the authors arrive at three key findings: Firstly, heteromeric paralogs of homomeric proteins are common, and are functionally more similar than paralogues of monomeric proteins. Secondly, in silico evolution suggests that negative selection acting on homomeric interfaces is sufficient to maintain heteromeric interactions between paralogs, but if selection acts only on one paralog, then the heteromeric interaction will slowly be lost. Finally, they show that diverging regulatory evolution (e.g. cell localization) can lead to relaxation of the structural constraints, thus enabling functional divergence.

Essential revisions:

1) Modeling of selection. The authors use the method previously described in Kachroo et al., 2015 to calculate the probability of fixation of new mutations; this is "an efficient implementation" of a model described by Sella and Hirsch, PNAS (2005). According to Kachroo et al., equation 3 is accurate as long as the product of the mutation rate and effective population size, N, is very small. Whilst this assumption is generally valid for wild yeast populations, in this study N is set to 1000 – several orders of magnitude lower than is realistic (Tsai et al., 2008). Using more plausible values for N, equation 3 would essentially guarantee fixation for beneficial mutations and vice versa, over-simplifying things. To address this issue, the authors should justify their choice of model and associated parameters and, ideally, demonstrate that their results are robust to changes in these parameters. It would be interesting to see if this affects the "selection on HET AB" case.

2) Analyses of age of duplication. Please clarify how the age of WGD paralogs was calculated, and whether this differs to the method used to calculate SSD ages. Are the two directly comparable? If not, then it might affect some of the conclusions (e.g. subsection “Paralogous heteromers frequently derive from ancestral homomers”). Similarly, people might take issue with the assumption that evolutionary rates are the same for SSDs vs. WGDs. A useful paper here might be Zhu et al., 2013.

3) Analysis of sequence divergence. I include one reviewer's description of this concern in its entirety, but both reviewers agreed with this concern: "In Figure 2E, fewer SSDs form HETs in general, compared to WGDs. This is probably related to the age of duplication events, as the authors note. The two groups of WGDs have the same age. But the SSDs would be from many different times. The authors mention that most SSDs are older, but it seems that some should still be relatively very young. Assuming that an ancestral gene whose protein homodimerizes undergoes a duplication event, the two duplicates should both homodimerize and heterodimerize among them. Accordingly, very young duplicates should belong mostly to group HM&HET. As time goes by, mutations and selection may separate them in two proteins that form only homodimers (group HM), or one of them still homodimerizes and the other evolves towards heterodimerization-only with the other paralogue. In Figure 2F, these two different cases of HM&HET are merged in one group.

I have major concerns about the sequence divergence analyses and their conclusions. First of all, we know that intrinsically disordered regions evolve fast, compared to well conserved domains. Also, some regions may function as flexible linkers (that also evolve fast) between domains. One protein family may evolve fast and another protein family may be very well conserved, irrespective of protein interactions. How do the authors control for this fact?

Moreover, the pleiotropic effect should be on the interaction surface or more broadly on the interaction domain that is responsible for the formation of the homomer or HTs. Usually, this is a well-defined domain or two. Usually, this interaction domain is one of the well conserved regions of the protein and many times a small part of it. I can't imagine how a sequence divergence analysis of the whole protein is meaningful. Maybe a PFAM analysis of the pairs of paralogues and inclusion only of the interacting domains instead of the whole protein? This is a problem. The crystallographic structures analysis they did in subsection “Paralogous heteromers frequently derive from ancestral homomers” is trying to address this problem, but I feel it may not be enough. Another concern is that intrinsically disordered regions are usually involved in transient interactions whereas domains are usually involved in more stable interactions, although this is not an absolute rule. Is this accounted for by the authors in their sequence divergence analyses? Probably not.

In my view, the level of sequence divergence of two paralogues is affected by their time of divergence, but also it is affected by the domain architecture of the protein and whether the interaction is transient or stable. Thus, the authors may need to control for them as well. Basically, the interaction surface/domain is under certain constraints. But other parts of the protein may evolve fast or slow for many other reasons.

Similar concerns exist for functional similarity analyses with GO, phenotypes and genetic interactions. A protein may have more than one functions that may be irrelevant with the formation of HMs and HETs. High functional similarity could only be due to short time after divergence. How do the authors control for that? In my opinion, although some statistically significant differences exist in the analyses of Figure 3, the final message is not clear and strong. "

4) In Figure 4, the positive and negative controls (panel B and C respectively) both behave as expected. However, I was surprised that selection to maintain the heteromer (D) appeared to be a stable state, as there seems to be no obvious reason why the homomers could not eventually be lost. In figures 4 and S9 it seems that the "selection on HET AB" panels seem to be noisier – is this coincidental?

5) This paper integrates data from many sources, which is a strong point. But at the same time, this makes it a lengthy paper, perhaps with too many analyses. At some points, it is easy to lose the main message of the paper and why the authors were doing a particular analysis. Please make the paper more clear and concise, possibly putting details of some analyses (or even some entire analyses) in the supplementary material.

6) Second paragraph of Results section discusses the effect of expression on detecting HMs by PCA. Since expression has an effect on detection of PPIs, is the difference of HMs among singletons, SSDs and WGDs (mentioned in subsection “Homomers and heteromers in the yeast PPI network”) due to this reason? Would it be feasible for the authors to collect subsets of singletons, SSDs and WGDs with similar magnitudes of expression (use bins) and check difference of HMs for these 3 controlled subsets?

7) Please clarify statistics in Supplementary file 2—table S5. More information should be included in that worksheet or somewhere else.

8) In Figure 2F, although there are some statistically significant differences, the various groups span similar orders of magnitude. Please comment on this observation.

9) Optional: Is it feasible for the authors to do an extra series of wet-lab experiments and experimentally test the HMs and HETs of a selected protein with crystal structure that underwent simulated evolution with the different selection scenarios? That would strengthen the paper further.

claims.claim: Gene duplication is a driver of the evolution of new functions.
claims.source: Gene duplication is a driver of the evolution of new functions.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about gene duplication.

claims.claim: The duplication of genes encoding homomeric proteins leads to the formation of homomers and heteromers of paralogs, creating new complexes after a single duplication event.
claims.source: The duplication of genes encoding homomeric proteins leads to the formation of homomers and heteromers of paralogs, creating new complexes after a single duplication event.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by the conceptual model presented in the manuscript and is a logical inference from the nature of protein duplication.

claims.claim: Heteromerization is frequent among duplicated homomers.
claims.source: Using yeast as a model, we find that heteromerization is frequent among duplicated homomers and correlates with functional similarity between paralogs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the PCA experiments and database analyses presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Heteromerization correlates with functional similarity between paralogs.
claims.source: Using yeast as a model, we find that heteromerization is frequent among duplicated homomers and correlates with functional similarity between paralogs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the functional analysis data presented in Figure 3 and related supplementary figures.

claims.claim: For homomers and heteromers sharing binding interfaces, mutations in one paralog can have structural pleiotropic effects on both interactions.
claims.source: Using in silico evolution, we show that for homomers and heteromers sharing binding interfaces, mutations in one paralog can have structural pleiotropic effects on both interactions, resulting in highly correlated responses of the complexes to selection.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the in silico evolution simulations presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: Mutations in one paralog result in highly correlated responses of the complexes to selection.
claims.source: Using in silico evolution, we show that for homomers and heteromers sharing binding interfaces, mutations in one paralog can have structural pleiotropic effects on both interactions, resulting in highly correlated responses of the complexes to selection.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through the in silico evolution experiments showing correlated binding energy changes.

claims.claim: Heteromerization could be preserved indirectly due to selection for the maintenance of homomers.
claims.source: Therefore, heteromerization could be preserved indirectly due to selection for the maintenance of homomers, thus slowing down functional divergence between paralogs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in silico evolution experiments showing that selection on homomers maintains heteromers.

claims.claim: Heteromerization slows down functional divergence between paralogs.
claims.source: Therefore, heteromerization could be preserved indirectly due to selection for the maintenance of homomers, thus slowing down functional divergence between paralogs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between heteromerization and functional similarity, and the simulation results.

claims.claim: Paralogs can overcome the obstacle of structural pleiotropy by regulatory evolution at the transcriptional and post-translational levels.
claims.source: We suggest that paralogs can overcome the obstacle of structural pleiotropy by regulatory evolution at the transcriptional and post-translational levels.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the analysis of expression correlation and localization data presented in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Proteins assemble into molecular complexes that perform and regulate structural, metabolic and signaling functions.
claims.source: Proteins assemble into molecular complexes that perform and regulate structural, metabolic and signaling functions (Janin et al., 2008; Marsh and Teichmann, 2015; Pandey et al., 2017; Scott and Pawson, 2009; Vidal et al., 2011; Wan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The assembly of complexes is necessary for protein function and thus constrains the sequence space available for protein evolution.
claims.source: The assembly of complexes is necessary for protein function and thus constrains the sequence space available for protein evolution.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on established knowledge about protein function and evolution.

claims.claim: A mutation in a given gene can have pleiotropic effects on other genes' functions through physical associations.
claims.source: One direct consequence of protein-protein interactions (PPIs) is that a mutation in a given gene can have pleiotropic effects on other genes' functions through physical associations.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of protein-protein interactions and is supported by established knowledge.

claims.claim: PPIs and pleiotropy may be particularly important during the evolution of new genes after duplication events.
claims.source: A context in which PPIs and pleiotropy may be particularly important is during the evolution of new genes after duplication events (Amoutzias et al., 2008; Baker et al., 2013; Diss et al., 2017; Kaltenegger and Ober, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on gene duplication and protein interactions.

claims.claim: The duplication of a homomeric protein leads not only to the formation of two homomers but also to a new heteromer.
claims.source: In this case, mutations in one paralog could have functional consequences for the other copy because the duplication of a homomeric protein leads not only to the formation of two homomers but also to a new heteromer (Figure 1) (Pereira-Leal et al., 2007; Wagner, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Among the 6070 tested yeast proteins, 1944 (32%) form homomers.
claims.source: We find that among the 6070 tested yeast proteins, 1944 (32%) form HMs, which agrees with previous estimates from crystal structures (Lynch, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data from PCA and database analyses.

claims.claim: The proportion of homomers among singletons (25%) is lower than for all duplicates: SSDs (38%), WGDs (33%), and 2D (38%).
claims.source: The proportion of HMs among singletons (n = 630, 25%) is lower than for all duplicates: SSDs (n = 980, 38%, p-value<2.0e-16), WGDs (n = 283, 33%, p-value=1.6e-05) and 2D (n = 51, 38%, p-value=1.7e-03) (Figure 2A Supplementary file 2 Tables S1 and S2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: There is a correlation between PCA signal and expression level, both at the level of mRNA and protein abundance.
claims.source: As previously observed (Celaj et al., 2017; Freschi et al., 2013), we found a correlation between PCA signal and expression level, both at the level of mRNA and protein abundance (Spearman's r = 0.33, p-value=3.5e-13 and Spearman's r = 0.46, p-value<2.2e-16 respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: When focusing only on previously reported homomers, we observed correlations between PCA signal and both mRNA and protein abundance.
claims.source: When focusing only on previously reported HMs, we also observed both correlations (Spearman's r = 0.37, p-value=3.9e-08 and Spearman's r = 0.38, p-value=6.0e-08 respectively).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data for known homomers.

claims.claim: There is a roughly two-fold increase in the probability of homomer detection when mRNA levels change by one order of magnitude.
claims.source: The association between PCA signal and expression translates into a roughly two-fold increase in the probability of HM detection when mRNA levels change by one order of magnitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the kernel regression analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Homomers reported in the literature but not detected by PCA have on average lower expression levels.
claims.source: Finally, we found that HMs reported in the literature but not detected by PCA have on average lower expression levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by the comparison of expression levels in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C.

claims.claim: Both SSDs and WGDs are more expressed than singletons at the mRNA and protein levels.
claims.source: We indeed observed that both SSDs and WGDs are more expressed than singletons at the mRNA and protein levels, with WGDs being more expressed than SSDs at the mRNA level (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claims.claim: Both expression level and duplication have significant effects on the probability of proteins to form homomers.
claims.source: However, expression level (and thus PPI detectability) does not explain completely the enrichment of HMs among duplicated proteins. Both factors, expression and duplication, have significant effects on the probability of proteins to form HMs (Supplementary file 2 Table S7. A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Supplementary file 2 Table S7. A.

claims.claim: When at least one paralog forms a homomer, the ancestral protein was also a homomer.
claims.source: Under the principle of parsimony, we can assume that when at least one paralog forms a HM, the ancestral protein was also a HM. This was shown to be true in general by Diss et al. (2017), who compared yeast WGDs to their orthologs from Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Diss et al. (2017) and the principle of parsimony.

claims.claim: When one homomer was observed in S. cerevisiae, at least one ortholog from pre-whole-genome duplication species formed a homomer.
claims.source: We confirm that when one HM was observed in S. cerevisiae, at least one ortholog from pre-whole-genome duplication species formed a HM (Figure 2B-C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the PCA experiments with orthologs shown in Figure 2B-C.

claims.claim: Most pairs forming heteromers also form at least one homomer (79%).
claims.source: Overall, most pairs forming HETs also form at least one HM (79%, Supplementary file 2 Table S3).
claims.evidence: This is based on the classification of interaction motifs from experimental data.

claims.claim: The majority of HM&HET pairs could be simple oligomers of paralogs that do not involve other proteins.
claims.source: However, we find that the majority of HM&HET pairs could be simple oligomers of paralogs that do not involve other proteins and are thus not part of large complexes. Only 70 (41%) of the 169 cases of HM&HET are in complexes with more than two distinct subunits among a set of 5535 complexes reported in databases (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of complex composition data from databases.

claims.claim: WGDs tend to form heteromers more often when they form at least one homomer, resulting in a larger proportion of HM&HET motifs than SSDs.
claims.source: We observed that the correlation between HM and HET formation is affected by whether paralogs are SSDs or WGDs (Figure 2E). WGDs tend to form HETs more often when they form at least one HM, resulting in a larger proportion of HM&HET motifs than SSDs.
claims.evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 2E comparing SSDs and WGDs.

claims.claim: The distribution of sequence divergence shows lower identity for SSDs than for WGDs.
claims.source: Indeed, we observed that the distribution of sequence divergence shows lower identity for SSDs than for WGDs, suggesting the presence of ancient duplicates that predate the whole-genome duplication (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequence identity analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claims.claim: Among SSDs, those forming HM&HET tend to show a marginally higher overall sequence identity.
claims.source: We indeed found that among SSDs, those forming HM&HET tend to show a marginally higher overall sequence identity (p=0.065, Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 5B and C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by the sequence identity comparison in Figure 2F and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: WGD pairs forming HM&HET show significantly higher sequence identity, albeit with a wider distribution.
claims.source: We also observed a significantly higher sequence identity for WGD pairs forming HM&HET, albeit with a wider distribution (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 5C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5C.

claims.claim: True ohnologs have a tendency to form heteromers more frequently than homeologs.
claims.source: For pairs whose ancestral state was a HM, we observed that true ohnologs have a tendency to form HET more frequently than homeologs (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is shown by the comparison in Figure 2E between homeologs and true ohnologs.

claims.claim: Homeologs are older than ohnologs, as shown by their lower pairwise sequence identity.
claims.source: Because homeologs had already diverged before the hybridization event, they are older than ohnologs, as shown by their lower pairwise sequence identity (Figure 2—figure supplement 5D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequence identity comparison in Figure 2—figure supplement 5D.

claims.claim: Pairwise amino acid sequence identity was higher for HM&HET than for HM pairs for both entire proteins and for their binding interfaces.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that pairwise amino acid sequence identity was higher for HM&HET than for HM pairs for both entire proteins and for their binding interfaces (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: The conservation ratio of the binding interface to the non-interface regions within the available structures is higher for those forming HM&HET.
claims.source: Furthermore, the conservation ratio of the binding interface to the non-interface regions within the available structures is higher for those forming HM&HET, suggesting a causal link between sequence identity at the interface and assembly of HM and HETs (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is shown by the relative conservation score analysis in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: 367 of 448 pairs of paralogs (82%) shared all their domain annotations.
claims.source: We found that 367 of 448 pairs of paralogs (82%) shared all their domain annotations (Supplementary file 2 Table S3).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of Pfam domain annotations.

claims.claim: HM&HET pairs are more similar than HM for SSDs in terms of GO terms, phenotypes, and genetic interactions.
claims.source: We found that HM&HET pairs are more similar than HM for SSDs (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the functional similarity analysis in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: For a similar level of sequence identity, HM&HET pairs have higher correlation of genetic interaction profiles than HM pairs.
claims.source: However, for a similar level of sequence identity, HM&HET pairs have higher correlation of genetic interaction profiles, higher GO molecular function (for SSDs) and higher GO biological process similarity (for both SSDs and WGDs) than HM pairs (Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and GLM test in Supplementary file 2 Table S7. B).
claims.evidence: This is shown by the GLM analysis controlling for sequence identity.

claims.claim: The retention of heteromers after the duplication of homomers appears to correlate with functional similarity, independently from sequence conservation.
claims.source: Overall, the retention of HETs after the duplication of HMs appears to correlate with functional similarity, independently from sequence conservation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional similarity analysis controlling for sequence identity.

claims.claim: Neutral evolution leads to the destabilization of all complexes derived from the simulated duplication of a homomer.
claims.source: We find that neutral evolution leads to the destabilization of all complexes derived from the simulated duplication of a HM (PDB: 1M38) (Figure 4B), as is expected given that there are more destabilizing mutations than stabilizing ones (Brender and Zhang, 2015; Guerois et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the in silico evolution simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Selection to maintain one homomer or both homomers significantly slows down the loss of the heteromer with respect to the neutral scenario.
claims.source: Selection to maintain one HM or both HMs significantly slows down the loss of the HET with respect to the neutral scenario (Figure 4C-E).
claims.evidence: This is shown by the simulation results in Figure 4C-E.

claims.claim: The heteromer is being destabilized more slowly than the second homomer when only one homomer is under negative selection.
claims.source: Interestingly, the HET is being destabilized more slowly than the second HM when only one HM is under negative selection.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the simulation results comparing the rates of destabilization.

claims.claim: Negative selection on heteromers significantly decelerates the loss of stability of both homomers.
claims.source: The reciprocal situation is also true, i.e. negative selection on HET significantly decelerates the loss of stability of both HMs (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The effects of single mutants on homomers and heteromers are strongly correlated and thus highly pleiotropic.
claims.source: By examining the effects that single mutants (only one of the loci gets a nonsynonymous mutation) have on HMs and HET, we find that, as expected, their effects are strongly correlated and thus highly pleiotropic (Pearson's r between 0.64 and 0.9 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4)).
claims.evidence: This is shown by the correlation analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Mutations tend to have greater effects on the homomer than on the heteromer.
claims.source: Additionally, mutations tend to have greater effects on the HM than on the HET (Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which agrees with observations on HMs having a greater variance of binding energies than HETs (André et al., 2008; Lukatsky et al., 2007; Lukatsky et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the mutational effect analysis and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The mutations sampled are slightly enriched for positive epistasis.
claims.source: Regardless of the selection scenario, the mutations sampled are slightly enriched for positive epistasis, since the slope values of regression models are smaller than one (0.91 and 0.89 under selection on HMs and HET respectively).
claims.evidence: This is shown by the epistasis analysis of double mutants.

claims.claim: Selection on the heteromer results in a further enrichment of mutations with positive epistasis.
claims.source: On the other hand, selection on the HET results in a further enrichment of mutations with positive epistasis (slope = 0.51, Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the epistasis analysis in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Epistasis may make heteromers more robust to mutations than homomers with respect to protein complex assembly.
claims.source: These observations suggest that epistasis may make HETs more robust to mutations than HMs with respect to protein complex assembly, contributing to their maintenance when the HMs are under selection and contributing to the loss of HMs when the HET is under negative selection.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis analysis and simulation results.

claims.claim: Expression profiles of paralogs are more correlated for both SSD and WGD paralogs forming HM&HET than for those forming only HM.
claims.source: These expression profiles are more correlated for both SSD and WGD paralogs forming HM&HET than for those forming only HM (p-value=6.5e-03 and 6.1e-03 respectively, Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the expression correlation analysis in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: For SSDs, co-expression shows significant effects on HM&HET formation when controlling for sequence identity.
claims.source: For SSDs, co-expression shows significant effects on HM&HET formation (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B. and Supplementary file 2 Table S7. B) but not for WGDs (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B. and Supplementary file 2 Table S7. B).
claims.evidence: This is shown by the GLM analysis in Figure 6C and supplementary materials.

claims.claim: HM&HET paralogs are more similar than HM for both SSDs and WGDs in terms of cellular compartments and cellular localization.
claims.source: Finally, we find that HM&HET paralogs are more similar than HM for both SSDs and WGDs in terms of cellular compartments (GO) and cellular localization derived from experimental data (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 3B C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the localization similarity analysis in Figure 6C and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: For a similar level of sequence identity, HM&HET pairs have higher cellular compartment and cellular localization similarity than HM pairs.
claims.source: For a similar level of sequence identity, HM&HET pairs have higher cellular compartment and cellular localization similarity (for both SSDs and WGDs) than HM pairs (Figure 6—figure supplement 4 and GLM test in Supplementary file 2 Table S7. B).
claims.evidence: This is shown by the GLM analysis controlling for sequence identity.

claims.claim: Most of the paralogs forming heteromers also form homomers.
claims.source: We found that most of the paralogs forming HETs also form HMs, suggesting that interactions between paralogs are inherited rather than gained de novo.
claims.evidence: This is based on the classification of interaction motifs from experimental data.

claims.claim: The HM&HET state can be more readily achieved by the duplication of an ancestral homomer rather than by the duplication of a monomeric protein followed by the gain of the homomers and of the heteromer.
claims.source: Accordingly, the HM&HET state can be more readily achieved by the duplication of an ancestral HM rather than by the duplication of a monomeric protein followed by the gain of the HMs and of the HET.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from models predicting interaction losses to be more likely than gains, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Interacting paralogs are more likely to derive from ancestral homomers.
claims.source: Interacting paralogs are therefore more likely to derive from ancestral HMs, as also shown by Diss et al. (2017) using limited comparative data.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Diss et al. (2017) and the data presented in this study.

claims.claim: An enrichment of homomers among yeast duplicated proteins compared to singletons has been reported in previous studies.
claims.source: We observed an enrichment of HMs among yeast duplicated proteins compared to singletons, as reported in previous studies (Ispolatov et al., 2005; Pereira-Leal et al., 2007; Pérez-Bercoff et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claims.claim: Analyses of PPIs from large-scale experiments have shown that interactions between paralogous proteins are more common than expected by chance.
claims.source: Also, analyses of PPIs from large-scale experiments have shown that interactions between paralogous proteins are more common than expected by chance (Ispolatov et al., 2005; Musso et al., 2007; Pereira-Leal et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous large-scale studies.

claims.claim: The duplication of homomeric proteins serves as a seed for the growth of protein complexes.
claims.source: Levy and Teichmann (2013) suggested that the duplication of HM proteins serves as a seed for the growth of protein complexes.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis from a previous study cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Cotranslational folding has been shown to be a problem for homomeric proteins because of premature assembly of protein complexes.
claims.source: Finally, cotranslational folding has been shown to be a problem for homomeric proteins because of premature assembly of protein complexes, particularly for proteins with interfaces closer to their N-terminus (Natan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Natan et al. (2018).

claims.claim: A large fraction of homomers and heteromers use the same binding interface.
claims.source: A large fraction of HMs and HETs use the same binding interface (Bergendahl and Marsh, 2017), so mutations at the interface may have pleiotropic effects on both HMs and HETs (Figure 1), which would lead to correlated responses to selection.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Bergendahl and Marsh (2017).

claims.claim: Natural selection would favor the maintenance of self-assembly if homomers need to self-interact in order to perform their function.
claims.source: If we assume that HMs need to self-interact in order to perform their function, it is expected that natural selection would favor the maintenance of self-assembly.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the assumption of functional necessity.

claims.claim: Negative selection on homomer interfaces would act on their pleiotropic residues and thus also preserve heteromer interfaces.
claims.source: Negative selection on HM interfaces would act on their pleiotropic residues and thus also preserve HET interfaces, preventing the loss of HETs as a correlated response.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the pleiotropic effects of mutations.

claims.claim: WGDs present proportionally more HM&HET motifs than SSDs.
claims.source: One of our observations is that WGDs present proportionally more HM&HET motifs than SSDs.
claims.evidence: This is based on the experimental data comparing SSDs and WGDs.

claims.claim: This is at least partly due to the age of paralogs, which would lead to more divergence.
claims.source: We propose that this is at least partly due to the age of paralogs, which would lead to more divergence.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the sequence identity data showing SSDs are older.

claims.claim: Upon a whole-genome duplication event, all subunits of complexes are duplicated at the same time, which may contribute to the increased retention of WGDs in complexes compared to SSDs.
claims.source: For instance, upon a whole-genome duplication event, all subunits of complexes are duplicated at the same time, which may contribute to the increased retention of WGDs in complexes compared to SSDs and thus maintain HETs.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of whole-genome duplication.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on stoichiometry.

claims.claim: SSDs display higher evolutionary rates than WGDs.
claims.source: In addition, SSDs display higher evolutionary rates than WGDs (Fares et al., 2013), which could lead to the faster loss of their interactions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Fares et al. (2013).

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Gagnon-Arsenault et al. (2013).

claims.claim: Paralogs that derive from homomers and that have lost their ability to form heteromers are less co-regulated and less co-localized.
claims.source: We found that paralogs that derive from HMs and that have lost their ability to form HETs are less co-regulated and less co-localized.
claims.evidence: This is based on the expression and localization analysis presented in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Duplication of self-interacting proteins creates paralogs whose evolution is constrained by pleiotropy in ways that are not expected for monomeric paralogs.
claims.source: Overall, our analyses show that duplication of self-interacting proteins creates paralogs whose evolution is constrained by pleiotropy in ways that are not expected for monomeric paralogs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall analysis of the manuscript.

claims.claim: Negative selection for the maintenance of heteromers of paralogs is not needed for their preservation.
claims.source: Another important result is that negative selection for the maintenance of heteromers of paralogs is not needed for their preservation, further enhancing our understanding of the role of non-adaptive evolution in shaping the complexity of cellular structures (Lynch et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results showing heteromers are maintained without direct selection.

results.result: The authors report that 32% of tested yeast proteins form homomers, with duplicated proteins (SSDs 38%, WGDs 33%, 2D 38%) showing significantly higher homomerization rates than singletons (25%). Both expression level and duplication status independently contribute to homomer formation probability.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 and C21-C22 are well-supported by experimental PCA data and statistical analyses (Figure 2A, Supplementary Tables). The enrichment of homomers among duplicates is statistically significant (p<2.0e-16 for SSDs), and GLM analysis confirms both expression and duplication have independent effects. The correlation with expression is appropriately acknowledged as a potential detection bias.

results.result: Heteromerization is frequent among duplicated homomers, with 79% of heteromer-forming pairs also forming at least one homomer. WGDs show proportionally more HM&HET motifs than SSDs, suggesting heteromers are inherited from ancestral homomers rather than gained de novo.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C25, C27, and C53 are supported by comprehensive PCA screening data covering 462 paralog pairs (Figure 2D-E, Supplementary Table S3). The classification of interaction motifs is systematic and the statistical comparisons between SSDs and WGDs are appropriate. The inference that heteromers are inherited is logically sound given the data.

results.result: The ancestral proteins of current paralog pairs that form homomers were themselves homomers, as demonstrated by parsimony arguments and experimental validation showing orthologs from pre-WGD species form homomers.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are supported by both logical inference (parsimony principle) and experimental validation using PCA with orthologs from L. kluyveri and Z. rouxii (Figure 2B-C). However, the experimental validation is limited to two paralog pairs, and some orthologs failed to show interactions, which could reflect technical limitations rather than true negatives.

results.result: Paralogs forming HM&HET show higher sequence identity than those forming only HM, particularly at binding interfaces. SSDs are generally older and more divergent than WGDs, and among WGDs, true ohnologs form heteromers more frequently than homeologs.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C35 are well-supported by sequence analysis and structural data (Figure 2F-H, Figure 2—supplements 5-6). The sequence identity analyses use appropriate phylogenetic data from PhylomeDB, and the structural interface analyses are based on crystallographic data. The relative conservation score analysis (C35) provides mechanistic insight, though the sample size for structures is limited (n=58 interfaces for yeast).

results.result: Heteromerization correlates with functional similarity between paralogs across multiple measures (GO terms, phenotypes, genetic interactions), and this correlation persists even when controlling for sequence identity.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C37-C39 are supported by comprehensive functional analyses using multiple independent datasets (Figure 3, Figure 3—supplements 2-4). The GLM analysis controlling for sequence identity (C38) is appropriate and strengthens the conclusion. However, some comparisons for WGDs show marginal or non-significant differences, which is appropriately noted.

results.result: In silico evolution simulations demonstrate that mutations at shared binding interfaces have pleiotropic effects on both homomers and heteromers (Pearson's r 0.64-0.9). Selection maintaining homomers significantly slows heteromer loss compared to neutral evolution, and reciprocally, selection on heteromers maintains homomers.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C40-C44 are supported by systematic in silico evolution simulations using FoldX on six high-quality crystal structures (Figure 4, Figure 4—supplements 2-4). The simulations appropriately model mutation sampling, selection, and fixation. The pleiotropic effects are quantified with strong correlations. However, the simulations are limited to interface mutations only and use specific parameter values (β=10, N=1000) that may not capture all biological scenarios.

results.result: Heteromers can be preserved indirectly through selection on homomers without requiring direct selection on the heteromer itself, potentially slowing functional divergence between paralogs through structural pleiotropy.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C62, and C74 represent the central mechanistic conclusion, supported by the integration of simulation results (Figure 4) showing correlated responses to selection and empirical observations of functional similarity correlating with heteromer retention. The logic is sound: pleiotropic mutations affecting shared interfaces maintain heteromers as a byproduct of homomer selection. This is a novel non-adaptive mechanism for heteromer maintenance.

results.result: Mutations show slightly positive epistasis overall (regression slopes 0.89-0.91), with stronger positive epistasis when heteromers are under selection (slope 0.51). This epistasis may make heteromers more robust to mutations than homomers.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 are supported by analysis of double mutants from simulations (Figure 5, Figure 5—supplements 1-3). The epistasis analysis is appropriate, comparing observed vs. expected effects on heteromers. The enrichment of positive epistasis under heteromer selection is statistically significant (t-test p=0.009). However, the mechanistic interpretation (C48) is somewhat speculative and would benefit from experimental validation.

results.result: Paralogs can overcome structural pleiotropy through regulatory evolution. HM&HET pairs show higher expression correlation and localization similarity than HM pairs, with co-expression showing significant effects on HM&HET formation for SSDs when controlling for sequence identity.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C49-C52, and C72 are supported by expression correlation analysis using microarray data across 1000+ conditions and localization data (Figure 6, Figure 6—supplements 1-4). The GLM analysis controlling for sequence identity is appropriate. However, the effect is significant only for SSDs, not WGDs (C50), and the mechanistic link between regulatory divergence and heteromer loss is correlative rather than causal.

results.result: PCA signal correlates with expression level (Spearman's r=0.33 for mRNA, r=0.46 for protein), with roughly two-fold increase in homomer detection probability per order of magnitude change in mRNA. Homomers not detected by PCA have lower expression levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C20 are well-supported by expression analysis of PCA data (Figure 2—supplement 1). The correlations are statistically significant and the kernel regression analysis appropriately quantifies the detection bias. This is important for interpreting the PCA results and acknowledging potential false negatives due to low expression.

results.result: The majority (59%) of HM&HET pairs are simple oligomers not part of large complexes, with only 41% found in complexes with more than two distinct subunits.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 is supported by analysis of complex composition using database annotations (5535 complexes). This finding is important for interpreting the biological significance of heteromers, suggesting many are not embedded in larger functional complexes. However, the analysis relies on database completeness and annotation quality.

results.result: 82% of paralog pairs (367 of 448) share all their Pfam domain annotations, with no significant difference in domain similarity between HM and HM&HET pairs.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 is supported by Pfam domain analysis (Supplementary Table S3, Figure 3—supplement 1). This negative result is important as it rules out domain gain/loss as a major mechanism for heteromer loss. The analysis is straightforward and appropriate.

results.result: WGDs show proportionally more HM&HET motifs than SSDs, which the authors attribute to the younger age of WGDs, preservation of stoichiometry during whole-genome duplication, lower evolutionary rates, and selection for gene dosage.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 integrate multiple observations and cite appropriate literature. The age explanation (C64) is supported by sequence identity data (C28). However, the relative contributions of different mechanisms (stoichiometry preservation C65-C66, evolutionary rates C67, dosage selection C68) are not quantitatively assessed, making this more of a discussion of possibilities than definitive conclusions.

results.result: Duplicated genes diverge quickly in transcriptional regulation due to cis-regulatory mutations, and this transcriptional divergence can directly change PPI profiles, as demonstrated by coding sequence swapping experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by appropriate citations to previous literature. These are established findings from prior work that provide context for the regulatory evolution hypothesis. The citation to Gagnon-Arsenault et al. (2013) for C71 is particularly relevant as direct experimental evidence.

results.result: Gene duplication drives evolution of new functions, and duplication of homomeric proteins creates both homomers and heteromers. Protein-protein interactions constrain evolution through pleiotropic effects, which is particularly important after duplication events.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C10-C14 represent established background knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. These provide the conceptual framework for the study. C2 and C14 specifically describe the model illustrated in Figure 1, which is the foundation for the entire investigation.

results.result: The HM&HET state is more readily achieved by duplication of ancestral homomers than by de novo gain. Previous studies have shown enrichment of homomers among duplicates and that interactions between paralogs are more common than expected by chance. Various adaptive hypotheses have been proposed for this enrichment.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C61 synthesize findings from previous literature with appropriate citations. These provide important context for interpreting the current results. The inference in C54 about the relative likelihood of different evolutionary paths is logical and supported by models cited (Gibson and Goldberg 2009, Presser et al. 2008).

results.result: Duplication of self-interacting proteins creates paralogs whose evolution is constrained by pleiotropy in ways not expected for monomeric paralogs.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is the overarching conclusion synthesizing all major findings. It is well-supported by the integration of empirical observations (heteromer frequency, functional similarity, sequence conservation) and simulation results (pleiotropic effects, correlated selection responses). This represents the main conceptual advance of the paper.
